runs.t: This manual replaces Chapter 18 of Todd Lammle, CCNA Certification Study Guide, Volume 2, Exam 200-301 (2020), book pages 495 to 548. It follows the book's order and numbering, keeps the book's learning objectives, and marks every place where this document differs from the book. Chapter 18 is a troubleshooting chapter: it tests whether you can find a fault step by step, so the labs and the troubleshooting tables matter more than usual.

Read it top to bottom: pre-check, sections 18.1 to 18.6, the chapter-wide troubleshooting table, labs, review questions, then the revision sheet and tracker table. Nothing here was run on real Cisco equipment. Where a command or output was not run, it is marked
495 to 548 (chapter text 495 to 543, Summary p. 544, Exam Essentials p. 545, Review Questions pp. 546 to 548). PDF pages 553 to 606 (offset +58, checked).

The book says most companies are on Windows 10 or upgrading from Windows 7. Windows 7 left support in January 2020 (general knowledge). Windows 10 reached end of support on

Why is an access point also called an endpoint?
It connects to the network (usually by wire) like any other device, even though it provides wireless access to others - vendors count it as an endpoint.
Why do office PCs often plug into the IP phone instead of the wall?
To save cabling and switch ports. The phone has a built-in switch - this is why the switch port carries a data VLAN and a voice VLAN.
Which endpoint types use wireless only, according to the book?
Mobile phones and tablets - desktops and laptops can use either.

Set speed and duplex by hand if autonegotiation fails (book p. 513)

Autonegotiation is on by default and is the normal practice. Set values by hand only when it fails.

The classic duplex mismatch happens when one end is set by hand to full duplex and the other is left on auto. The auto end cannot see the setting, falls back to half duplex, and the two ends disagree.
Rule: both ends auto, or both ends fixed to the same values. Never one of each.

Cisco's own wording says a duplex mismatch is a common cause of these errors; cabling and faulty ports cause them too, so "most common" is a fair rule of thumb but not a law. A traffic sniffer is a great troubleshooting tool, but on a switch it sees little. A switch sends unicast frames only out of the port where the destination MAC address lives, so a sniffer on another port cannot see them. (A hub sent everything to all ports, so sniffers worked there.)
the traffic of a source port to a destination port, where you plug in the analyser.

The switch forwards unicast frames only to the port where the destination MAC address is - a hub sent everything to every port.
